If your Apple CarPlay connection suddenly drops while driving, the problem may not lie with your iPhone, the cable, or your car.

Instead, it could be caused by radio interference.

A previous Axios report detailed a strange phenomenon in Boston, where drivers lost CarPlay or Android Auto connections when passing through specific locations. Similar "signal dead zones" may exist in other cities, but no one has reported them.

The CarPlay head unit cannot handle GPS navigation on its own; it maintains a direct connection with your iPhone via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, then mirrors the display. Everything on screen relies on your phone's internet and GPS satellite signals. When the wireless connection between the head unit and the phone is interfered with, navigation fails and the connection may drop.

In Grapevine, Texas, I know of a specific stretch of road, sandwiched between an oil depot and a nursing home, where all wireless CarPlay systems crash when driving through it. I've tried several vehicles, including those with factory-equipped wireless CarPlay, wireless CarPlay adapters, and aftermarket audio systems—all of them stall on this stretch. Some systems recover on their own after interference, others don't. Even the latest Mercedes-Benz electric cars have this issue.

In the past ten years, I've only encountered this situation a handful of times.

Experts point out that nearby radio sources—especially signals on the 2.4GHz band—may be the source of interference. In Boston's case, suspects could include point-to-point microwave links, broadcast antennas, or unlicensed transmitting devices.

The most important point is: if you keep losing CarPlay connection at the same location, you may be driving through an invisible radio interference zone. This problem may not be solvable, but knowing the cause can save you considerable time—no need to search endlessly for the reason, and no need to book unnecessary repair services.
